title: Process Control - Common Terms
description: A comprehensive reference guide for common terminology used in process control systems, including definitions of analog/digital signals, controller modes, PID components, and key process control concepts.

rows: Electrical signals like voltage or electric current representing temperature, pressure, or level. Typically 4-20 mA where 4 mA is minimum and 20 mA is maximum span.
Electronic hardware that converts analog signals like voltage, current, temperature, or pressure into digital data for computer processing.
Controller mode where output is calculated using the error signal - the difference between set point and process variable.
Two or more controllers working together where the master controller's output becomes the set point for the slave controller.
Standard Microsoft OS method for communication between applications. Replaced by OLE/OPC for process control.
Range through which an input can be varied without initiating a response.
Time duration for the process variable to start changing after changing an output (control valve, VFD, etc.).
Derivative part of PID controller where output is proportional to rate of change of process variable or error.
Term commonly used instead of dead time.
Any departure from a desired or expected process value.
Discrete binary value with two states (1 or 0), often used for on-off indication.
Larger digital control systems for process management.
On or off signals sent or received to the field.
Control system where controller elements are distributed throughout rather than centrally located.
Process where lag time is larger than dead time. Most process plant loops are dominant lag types including temperature, level, flow, and pressure loops.
In control loop: Error = Set Point - Process Value.
Calculated as 100 / Proportional Band. Higher gain provides faster loop response but more oscillatory/unstable process. Process Gain = change in output / change in input.
Difference in logarithms of amplitude ratios at frequency where combined phase angle is 180 degrees lag.
Signal change required before output unit (valve or similar) moves.
Electronic hardware where field devices are wired.
Integral part of PID controller where output is proportional to amount and duration of error signal.
Process upset not caused by changing the set-point.
Time after dead time that process variable takes to move 63.3% of final value after step change in valve position.
Controller mode where output is set manually.
Controller setting: auto, manual, or remote mode.
Software that process operator uses to operate the process.
Amount a process exceeds the set point during system load change or set point change.
Controller including Proportional, Integrating, and Derivative functions per ANSI/IEEE Standard 100-1977.
Actual value in control loop: temperature, pressure, flow, composition, pH, etc.
Controllers replacing relay logic, usually with PID controller functions.
Actual value in control loop including temperature, pressure, flow, composition, pH, etc.
Controller output proportional to error or process variable change. Proportional Band = 100 / Gain.
Same as derivative or D part of PID controllers.
Data storage location in a PLC.
Controller that changes output variable to move process variable back to set point.
Variation in outputs for the same change of input.
Same as integral or I part of PID controllers.
Integral action continuing to change controller output after actual output reaches physical limit.
Rate at which controller samples process variable and calculates new output.
Desired value of the process variable.
Senses actual system value and transforms it to standardized signal (typically 4-20 mA for analog signals) as input to control system.
